rv.q: The atmosphere around Heisenberg is charged with more electricity than Ben Franklin ever dreamed of.
They're the sexiest couple on a New York stage just now.
The actors are back, even more nuanced and riveting, at MTC’s Broadway venue, subtly peeling layers off a vastly improbable yet profoundly believable relationship.
It makes that smallness feel liberating.
Parker is Georgie, a 42-year-old American expat in London: a self-consciously weird oversharer and possible grifter.
There's something generously honest in 'Heisenberg' about ordinariness.
It is, in fact, blush-makingly trite, a portrait of a 42-year-old blabbermouth who stalks a never-married 75-year-old butcher and lures him into the sack.
Simon Stephens' remarkable Heisenberg generates all the potency and disarming immediacy on Broadway that it conjured off Broadway.
What seems so incredibly simplistic somehow registers as one of the most emotionally complex relationships you’re likely to witness on stage or in real life.
Like their relationship, “Heisenberg” is more than the sum of its parts.
Ms. Parker has never been better.

Presumably, playwright Simon Stephens, Tony winner for Incident of the Dog in the Night-Time, named this work for the aforementioned theoretical physicist, whose uncertainty principle is known for having redefined physics, much in the way Georgie and Alex help to redefine each other.
Well, perhaps not — but it was a privilege to share it with them, to spend some time with two very human human beings.
The Emmy and Tony Award-winning Parker plays the character with an explosive near-perfection.
If Mary Louise Parker's Georgie had asked me as well as Denis Arndt's Alex whether I found her exhausting but captivating, my answer would have been a resounding yes.

And it's indeed a quite charming smile Arndt displays in a gracefully strong performance, mixing good-natured, gentle humor with a fear of the hurt that may result from opening up his heart once more.
I am certain that these actors' sterling work is not to be missed.
Parker and Arndt keep us deeply invested in each of their erratic movements.
'Heisenberg' is not rocket science — or particle physics. It's just a sweet story about two people who think they don't deserve love.
Parker makes her an ultimately fetching kook, a free spirit who marches to the beat of a different drummer — who happens to be improvising.
There’s a nagging difference, that’s for certain.

Because Stephens doesn't make that case, the evening becomes more about the artifice of its creation than the relationship it documents, and despite its intriguing, understated premise (the title is never directly explained), it just isn't written well enough to function in that capacity.
Even though 'Heisenberg' is directed with efficiency by Mark Brokaw and has its share of smart, charming dialogue, I grew weary.
As it happens, the play itself is just as thin as the production values.
“Heisenberg” is not one of those screwball comedies in which opposites attract.
Ms. Parker is a truthful actor, but playwright Stephens has created a character that is hard to root for, much less wish love, strange or otherwise.

Everything about “Heisenberg,” in short, is fake, including its title, a pretentious allusion to physicist Werner Heisenberg’s uncertainty principle in quantum mechanics, which the playwright obviously doesn’t understand.
And this "random" human encounter leads to a most bizarre connection and a most revealing evening of electrifying theater.
Parker and Arndt are two sure contenders for accolades in next year’s Tony season, making Heisenberg an evening of theatre you don’t want to miss.

Alex, passive and long celibate (his last name, after all, is Priest) surprises us with his long-dormant humor and sensuality. Georgie, with her charming take-no-prisoners, scorched earth personality (last name, Burns), relaxes enough to want to please Alex.
There is no uncertainty that this is a captivating play offering two highly appealing performances.
Heisenberg meets the vicissitudes of the human condition and clarity convenes on the stage of life and on the stage of the Samuel J. Friedman Theatre.
What's truly wonderful about 'Heisenberg' is that it never goes where you expect it to go...Yet, it all feels completely believable because of the performances of these two masterful actors.
Parker turns in an astonishing performance
The result is exquisite – delicate in its observation of two damaged souls stumbling their way to the other.
Stephens, who, I am convinced, can do just about anything brilliantly, has mastered the genre.

Their idiosyncrasies and traits are strikingly rendered with both performers giving skillful, nuanced portrayals. However, the overall thrust of the production, while bewitching and absorbing, is modest at best. Mary Louise-Parker and Denis Ardnt deliver two outstanding performances.

If the play's first half feels less engaging because of how much remains unknown (Why is she low-key stalking him? Is everything she says a lie? What is the point of all this?), by the end it subtly poses much larger questions you're likely to think about for some time afterward.

Which explains how Parker overcomes Georgie’s volatile, inherently annoying demeanor to make this role captivating, particularly in contrast with Arndt’s reclusive Irish bachelor, who lives in a large house, holding imaginary conversations with his sister who died when he was a child.
He now takes the story in a different direction and makes a point that is sparkling new – and worth hearing.
You may find her captivating but her self-involved chatter is definitely exhausting.

Heisenberg, a slender two-hander starring Mary-Louise Parker and Dennis Arndt as May-December lovers, while not up to the best of his previous work, nonetheless satisfactorily fills 80 intermissionless minutes at the Samuel J. Friedman Theatre.

Simon Stephens’ Heisenberg, likely named after the uncertain relationship in which these two find themselves, is a gentle and unassuming play, one whose eighty minutes pass without much surprise but without much to dissatisfy, either.
By resorting to tropes fast becoming standard in contemporary non-musical plays, it becomes remote, and unsatisfyingly predictable.
I couldn't tell where the play was going or why it even started in the first place.
A one-act, bare-bones look at the baffling interactions between two underwritten characters, 'Heisenberg' offers a pretentiously philosophical take on the myth of the manic pixie dream girl.

Of all the two-character plays that have come out in the last decade, Heisenberg has got to be one of the most provocative dramas of bringing two diametrically opposed people together, and is certainly one of the best.
What Georgie does is jump start his life, as this play puts the audience to sleep.

cn.t: Critics are divided on this minimalist two-hander: Parker and Arndt earn widespread praise for their performances, but many find Stephens' brief romantic drama underwritten, overly quirky, and uncertain in purpose despite its intimate staging.
